findings.why: The earliest dated record is at 2026-07-09 13:29 UTC, 14.5 h after this moment (2026-07-08 23:00 UTC). Whatever happened before it is outside what the release dates.

findings.why: The latest dated record is at 2026-07-13 15:50 UTC, 2.2 h after this moment (2026-07-13 13:37 UTC): activity continues after the moment the report names.

findings.why: The latest dated record is at 2026-07-13 15:50 UTC, 5.8 days before this moment (2026-07-19 12:03 UTC): the release does not reach it.

findings.finding: About 1,200 agents were on the message board.
findings.why: The records carry tokens and self-chosen names, not agents. This release has 241 named actors and 77,626 runs with no name, and no field that says which agent a record came from, so an agent count cannot be read from it.

findings.finding: About 700 agents joined the Hugging Face attack.
findings.why: Counting agents in the attack needs the same missing mapping from records to agents (241 named actors and 77,626 anonymous runs are what the records show).

findings.finding: The board holds more than 70,000 messages and files (about 63,000 messages and about 6,000 files in a 1.2 million entry dump).
findings.why: The board's contents are not in the release. Only the folders that payload code names are visible: 503 board places, with 0 messages the tool can pair between named actors.

findings.finding: The main namespace holds at least 95% of the messaging done through Artifactory.
findings.why: 5% of the channel operations the tool finds are on board places (503 folders). The release shows the board only through the code that names its folders, so what share of all messaging it holds cannot be tested here.

findings.finding: All 11 of the top attack coordinators exited by early 12 July.
findings.why: Naming the coordinators needs agent identities and a coordinator rating from the board. The release has neither. Only the time of the mass exit is visible (see the finding above).

findings.source: OpenAI TR p.9, p.34 (METR p.35 says two working credentials)
findings.finding: 14 exposed Hugging Face user tokens were posted to the board on 10 July.
findings.why: Credentials are redacted to placeholders and the post itself is on the board, which is not in the release, so how many tokens were posted or which worked cannot be read.

findings.finding: Agent code ran on 41 Hugging Face production dataset workers.
findings.why: Hugging Face infrastructure details are redacted, so workers cannot be told apart or counted.

findings.finding: From 13 July at least 19 agents sent 429 signed board messages.
findings.why: Signed messages are board entries. Board contents are not in the release.

findings.finding: Agents used HOLD, VETO, owner and STOP conventions to manage shared resources.
findings.why: No record in the release matches.

findings.finding: 181 VPN device enrollments with the stolen key.
findings.why: 154 records run or prepare an enrollment. A record is one attempt written in code, not one enrollment that succeeded, so the count and the 181 are different things.

findings.source: METR p.14, p.33; OpenAI TR p.16

findings.why: 11 records mention the sandbox host.

findings.finding: About 7% of transcripts had spoofed tool calls, all small obvious tests.

findings.finding: 7,905 agent names against about 1,200 agents: names are self-chosen and changed often.
findings.why: The Agents tab proposes which tokens and names are probably one agent from counted evidence (241 named actors, 77,626 anonymous runs), and the sensitivity section shows how much the answers move. It cannot recover the true number.

grading.why: Chosen before the grading was re-run, and not from the tool's own error. One hour is the margin the validation suite already uses for 'a sign is on time' and the floor the old rule had; the published times are given to the minute. Disclosure: the author who set it had seen the differences from the earlier runs (about 0.2 to 2.2 hours for the seven milestones), so this is fixed in advance of this run, not blind to the earlier ones. A fully blind grading needs findings and a tolerance written by someone who has not seen the output.
grading.previous_rule: v2.1.0 used the 90th-percentile fit error of the tool's own worst timed block (5.05 h on the release), so the worse the dating, the more findings counted as recovered.
grading.circular_why: A 'claim' or 'text_count' check asks whether text the Swarm Traces authors cite is in their own release, and the pack's handle list was written from the same report, so 'recovered' there means 'the pattern is present', not that the tool found something unknown. 'static' findings are invisible by definition. Quote the time-based and per-day checks as the test; report the rest separately.

about: What the incident's insiders (METR, OpenAI, Hugging Face) and the Swarm Traces authors found, taken only from agenttrace/claims/incident_context.json, incident_milestones.json and swarm_traces_report.json, each with the source the claim files cite. Each finding is checked against the loaded records by agenttrace.sensitivity: recovered (the tool shows it, within its dating error), partly (some of it shows) or invisible (the records cannot show it). Statuses, evidence and numbers are computed live; 'why_static' is text for findings whose status cannot be computed, with {placeholders} filled from the loaded data.

status_rule.recovered: for a time: within the fixed tolerance in grading.tolerance_h (1 h), whatever the tool's own dating error; for a count: within a quarter either way, or all cited records found and matching
status_rule.partly: for a time: within 24 h, or the thing is found at a different size; for a count or claim: some records show it
status_rule.invisible: not found, outside the dated range of the release, or needs data the records do not hold
